Now the square on AC and the rectangle AC·CB are under the same height AC, so that the square on AC is to the rectangle AC·CB as AC is to CB [6.1]; therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with the rectangle AC·CB [10.11]. But the sum of the squares on AC, CB is commensurable with the square on AC (Step 5); therefore the sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with the rectangle AC·CB [10.13]. And twice the rectangle AC·CB is commensurable with the rectangle AC·CB (Step 6); therefore twice the rectangle AC·CB is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AC, CB [10.13]; that is, HG is incommensurable with EG. In exactly the same way, AD being incommensurable in length with DB, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD·DB [6.1, 10.11, 10.13]; that is, HI is incommensurable with EI.

**Step 8.** Now EG and HG are rectangles under the same height EF; therefore EG is to HG as EM is to HM [6.1]. And EG is incommensurable with HG; therefore EM is incommensurable in length with HM [10.11]. Similarly EI is to HI as EN is to HN [6.1], and EI is incommensurable with HI; therefore EN is incommensurable in length with HN [10.11].

**Step 9.** Further, EM and HM are each rational and incommensurable in length with EF (Steps 5, 6); therefore each of them is commensurable in square with EF [D10.1.3], that is, the square on EM and the square on HM are each commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.2]; hence the square on EM is commensurable with the square on HM [10.12], so that EM, HM are commensurable in square. Combining this with Step 8, EM and HM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore EH, the remainder when HM is subtracted from EM, is an apotome, and HM is a rational straight line annexed to it which is commensurable with the whole EM in square only [10.73]. By the same argument EN and HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [D10.1.3, D10.1.2, 10.12], so that EH, the remainder when HN is subtracted from EN, is an apotome with HN annexed to it, HN being commensurable with the whole EN in square only [10.73].

**Step 10.** But HN is not the same straight line as HM. For since AC is a part of AD and CB is a part of DB (Step 2), the rectangle AC·CB is a part of the rectangle AD·DB, so that the rectangle AD·DB is greater than the rectangle AC·CB, and twice the rectangle AD·DB is greater than twice the rectangle AC·CB [CN5]; that is, HI is greater than HG. Now HI and HG are under the same height EF, so that HI is to HG as HN is to HM [6.1]; and HI is greater than HG; therefore HN is greater than HM [5.14]. Thus HM and HN are different straight lines.

**Step 11.** Therefore to the apotome EH there have been annexed two different rational straight lines, HM and HN, each of which is commensurable with the whole in square only. But to an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only [10.79]: which is impossible. Therefore the supposition is false, and no medial straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB which is commensurable with the whole in square only and contains with the whole a medial rectangle.

Therefore to a second apotome of a medial straight line only one medial straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only and which contains with the whole a medial rectangle. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To a minor straight line only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which makes, with the whole, the sum of the squares on them rational but twice the rectangle contained by them medial.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a minor straight line. By 10.76, AB is the remainder obtained when from a straight line AC there is subtracted a straight line CB which is incommensurable in square with AC and which makes with AC the sum of the squares on AC, CB rational but twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB medial. Thus BC is an annex to AB: the point B lies between A and C, AC is the whole, CB is the annex, and AC, CB satisfy the stated conditions. [10.76]

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that a different straight line BD can also be so annexed to AB, so that D lies on AB produced beyond B, D is distinct from C, AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is rational, and twice the rectangle contained by AD, DB is medial.

**Step 3.** Since C and D both lie on AB produced beyond B and are distinct points, the straight lines AC, AD are unequal. Let AD be the greater; if AC is the greater, the same argument applies with the letters C and D interchanged, since the conditions imposed on AC, CB and on AD, DB are identical. Then C lies between B and D, so that AD is cut at C into the segments AC, CD, and DB is cut at C into the segments DC, CB.

**Step 4.** Since DB is cut at C, the rectangle contained by AD, DB is equal to the rectangles contained by AD, DC and by AD, CB [2.1]; therefore the rectangle AD, DB is greater than the rectangle AD, CB [CN5]. Again, since AD is cut at C, the rectangle contained by AD, CB is equal to the rectangles contained by AC, CB and by CD, CB [2.1]; therefore the rectangle AD, CB is greater than the rectangle AC, CB [CN5]. Hence the rectangle AD, DB is greater than the rectangle AC, CB, and consequently twice the rectangle AD, DB is greater than twice the rectangle AC, CB. Let R be the area by which twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB, so that twice the rectangle AD, DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with R.

**Step 5.** Since AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Likewise, since AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with the square on AB [2.7]. Let X denote the sum of the squares on AD, DB, Y the sum of the squares on AC, CB, P twice the rectangle AD, DB, and Q twice the rectangle AC, CB; then X is equal to P together with the square on AB, and Y is equal to Q together with the square on AB.

**Step 6.** By Step 4, P is equal to Q together with R. Adding R to the equals Y and Q together with the square on AB [CN2], Y together with R is equal to Q, the square on AB and R together; and this is P together with the square on AB, which is X (Step 5). Therefore X is equal to Y together with R [CN1]; that is, the squares on AD, DB exceed the squares on AC, CB by the very same area R by which twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB.

**Step 7.** Now the sum X of the squares on AD, DB is rational (Step 2), and the sum Y of the squares on AC, CB is rational (Step 1); that is, each of X and Y is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4]. Therefore X and Y, being commensurable with the same area, are commensurable with one another [10.12].

**Step 8.** Since the whole X is made up of the two parts Y and R (Step 6), and the whole X is commensurable with one of the parts, namely Y (Step 7), the two parts Y and R are commensurable with one another [10.15]. But Y is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out (Step 7); therefore R is also commensurable with that square [10.12], and so R is a rational area [D10.1.4].

**Step 9.** But twice the rectangle AD, DB is medial (Step 2) and twice the rectangle AC, CB is medial (Step 1), and by Step 4 the former exceeds the latter by the area R, which has been shown to be rational (Step 8). Thus a medial area would exceed a medial area by a rational area; which is impossible [10.26].

**Step 10.** Therefore no straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB which is incommensurable in square with the whole and which makes with the whole the sum of the squares on them rational but twice the rectangle contained by them medial. Hence to a minor straight line only one such straight line can be annexed. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial, but twice the rectangle contained by them rational.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole, and let BC be a straight line annexed to AB, so that AC is the whole straight line and CB the annex. By 10.77, AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is rational.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that a second straight line BD, different from BC, can also be annexed to AB with the same properties: AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial, and twice the rectangle AD, DB is rational (10.77). Since BC and BD are unequal, let BD be the greater; then C lies between B and D, so AC is a part of AD and CB a part of DB, whence AD is greater than AC and DB greater than CB (CN5). Consequently the square on AD is greater than the square on AC and the square on DB is greater than the square on CB, the lesser square being a part of the greater (CN5); so the sum of the squares on AD, DB exceeds the sum of the squares on AC, CB by some area. Call this excess E.

**Step 3.** Since AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB (2.7). Likewise, since AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB (2.7).

**Step 4.** By Step 2, the squares on AD, DB are equal to the squares on AC, CB together with E. Replacing each sum of squares by the equal area found in Step 3 (CN1), twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB and E. Subtracting the common square on AB from both (CN3), twice the rectangle AD, DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with E. Thus twice the rectangle AD, DB exceeds twice the rectangle AC, CB by the same area E by which the squares on AD, DB exceed the squares on AC, CB.

**Step 5.** E is a rational area. Let K be the square on the rational straight line set out. Twice the rectangle AD, DB is rational and is therefore commensurable with K, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is rational and is therefore commensurable with K (D10.1.4). Hence twice the rectangle AD, DB is commensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB (10.12). Now twice the rectangle AD, DB is the whole composed of the two parts twice the rectangle AC, CB and E, and this whole is commensurable with the part twice the rectangle AC, CB; therefore the parts are commensurable, that is, E is commensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB (10.15). Since twice the rectangle AC, CB is commensurable with K, E is also commensurable with K (10.12), and therefore E is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 6.** Therefore the sum of the squares on AD, DB, which is a medial area, exceeds the sum of the squares on AC, CB, which is also a medial area, by the rational area E. But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area (10.26). This is impossible.

**Step 7.** Hence no straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB so as to be incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and to make with the whole the sum of the squares on them medial but twice the rectangle contained by them rational. Therefore to a straight line which produces with a rational area a medial whole only one such straight line can be annexed. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them both medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole, and let BC be the straight line annexed to it, so that AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, twice the rectangle AC, CB is medial, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AC, CB [10.78]. I say that no other straight line can be annexed to AB satisfying the same conditions.

**Step 2.** For suppose, if possible, that BD, a straight line different from BC, is also annexed to AB, so that AD and DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial, twice the rectangle AD, DB is medial, and the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD, DB.

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line EF [D10.1.3]. To EF apply a rectangle EG equal to the sum of the squares on AC, CB, producing EM as breadth [1.44, 1.45]; and from EG cut off, on the same side EF, a rectangle HG equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB, producing HM as breadth [1.44, 1.45]. Let EL be the remaining rectangle, with breadth EH.

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AC is cut at B, the squares on AC, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on AB [2.7]. But EG is equal to the squares on AC, CB, and HG is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB; therefore EG is equal to HG together with the square on AB [CN1]. Taking away HG from both, the remainder EL is equal to the square on AB [CN3].

**Step 5.** Again, to EF apply a rectangle EI equal to the sum of the squares on AD, DB, producing EN as breadth [1.44, 1.45]. Since AB is less than AD, the square on AB, that is EL, is less than EI [CN5]; both being applied to EF from the point E, EL is a part of EI and H falls between E and N. Since AD is cut at B, the squares on AD, DB together are equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on AB [2.7]; that is, EI is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with EL [CN1]. Taking away EL from both, the remainder HI is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB [CN3], and its breadth is HN.

**Step 6.** The sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line [10.21]; and EG is equal to it. Thus EG, the square on a medial straight line, is applied to the rational straight line EF producing EM as breadth; therefore EM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Likewise twice the rectangle AC, CB is medial and HG is equal to it, so that HG is the square on a medial straight line applied to EF producing HM as breadth; therefore HM is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 7.** Since the sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB, and EG, HG are equal to these respectively, EG is incommensurable with HG. Now EG and HG are rectangles of the same height EF standing on the bases EM, HM; therefore, as EG is to HG, so is EM to HM [6.1]. Since the first is incommensurable with the second, EM is incommensurable in length with HM [10.11].

**Step 8.** EM and HM are each rational and each incommensurable in length with EF; hence each is commensurable in square only with EF [D10.1.3], so that the squares on EM and on HM are each commensurable with the square on EF and therefore with one another [10.12]; that is, EM and HM are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Together with Step 7, EM and HM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore EH, the remainder when HM is subtracted from EM, is an apotome, and HM is its annex [10.73].

**Step 9.** In the same way, EI is equal to the sum of the squares on AD, DB, which is medial, and is applied to EF producing EN; therefore EN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. HI is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB, which is medial, and is applied to EF producing HN; therefore HN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Since the sum of the squares on AD, DB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AD, DB, EI is incommensurable with HI; and, as EI is to HI, so is EN to HN [6.1]; therefore EN is incommensurable in length with HN [10.11]. Moreover EN and HN, being rational and each commensurable in square only with EF, are commensurable in square with one another [D10.1.3, 10.12, D10.1.2]. Therefore EN, HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and EH, the remainder when HN is subtracted from EN, is an apotome with HN as its annex [10.73].

**Step 10.** The annexes HM and HN are different. For BD is not equal to BC; let BD be the greater (the other case is treated in the same way). Then AD is greater than AC and DB is greater than CB, so the sum of the squares on AD, DB is greater than the sum of the squares on AC, CB [CN5]; that is, EI is greater than EG. If EN were equal to EM, the rectangles EI and EG, applied to the same EF from the same point E, would coincide and be equal [CN4]; therefore EN is not equal to EM. And if HN were equal to HM, then, the common EH being added to each, EN would be equal to EM [CN2]; therefore HN is not equal to HM.

**Step 11.** Thus to the apotome EH two different rational straight lines, HM and HN, have been annexed, each commensurable in square only with the corresponding whole EM or EN. But to an apotome only one rational straight line can be annexed which is commensurable with the whole in square only [10.79]. This is impossible; therefore no straight line other than BC can be annexed to AB satisfying the conditions of Step 2.

**Step 12.** Therefore to a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole only one straight line can be annexed which is incommensurable in square with the whole straight line and which with the whole straight line makes the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them both medial and also incommensurable with the sum of the squares on them. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To find the first apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the rational straight line set out (D10.1.3), and let BG be a straight line commensurable in length with A. Then BG, being commensurable with the rational straight line A, is itself rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 2.** Let two square numbers DE, EF be taken, the point F lying between D and E so that DE is made up of DF and FE, and such that the difference DF is not a square number: namely, let DE be the number 9, which is 3 multiplied by 3, and EF the number 4, which is 2 multiplied by 2, so that both are square numbers (D7.18); then DF is the number 5, which is not square, since 2 by 2 makes 4 and 3 by 3 makes 9, and no number lies between 2 and 3, so that no number multiplied by itself makes 5. Also ED is greater than DF, since DF is a part of DE.

**Step 3.** ED has not to DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number. For if it had, then, since the first, ED, is a square number, the second, DF, would also be a square number (8.24); but DF is not square (Step 2).

**Step 4.** Using the numbers ED, DF and the straight line BG, let a straight line X be found, by the Porism to 10.6, such that, as the number ED is to the number DF, so is the square on BG to the square on X (10.6): a straight line Y is found such that BG is to Y as ED is to DF, and X is taken as a mean proportional between BG and Y, so that BG is to Y as the square on BG is to the square on X.

**Step 5.** Since, as ED is to DF, so is the square on BG to the square on X, take the doubles of ED and of the square on BG (equimultiples of the first and third) and the doubles of DF and of the square on X (equimultiples of the second and fourth). Since ED is greater than DF (Step 2), the double of ED exceeds the double of DF; therefore, by the definition of magnitudes in the same ratio, the double of the square on BG exceeds the double of the square on X (D5.5). Hence the square on BG is greater than the square on X, and therefore BG is greater than X; for if X were equal to or greater than BG, the square on X would be equal to or greater than the square on BG.

**Step 6.** From the greater straight line GB let GC be cut off equal to the less, X (1.3), so that C lies on BG between B and G, and BC is the remainder when GC is subtracted from BG. Since GC is equal to X, the square on GC is equal to the square on X; therefore, as the number ED is to the number DF, so is the square on BG to the square on GC, and BG is greater than GC.

**Step 7.** Since the square on BG has to the square on GC the ratio which the number ED has to the number DF, the square on BG is commensurable with the square on GC (10.6).

**Step 8.** Since BG is commensurable in length with A, the square on BG has to the square on A the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and therefore the ratio which a number has to a number; hence the square on BG is commensurable with the square on A (10.6). But the square on GC is commensurable with the square on BG (Step 7). Therefore the square on GC is commensurable with the square on A (10.12); that is, GC is commensurable in square with A (D10.1.2), and so GC is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 9.** Since ED has not to DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 3), and the square on BG has to the square on GC the same ratio as ED has to DF (Step 6), neither has the square on BG to the square on GC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BG is incommensurable in length with GC (10.9). Thus BG, GC are rational straight lines (Steps 1, 8) which are commensurable in square (Step 7, D10.1.2) but incommensurable in length, that is, commensurable in square only.

**Step 10.** Therefore, since from the rational straight line BG there has been subtracted the rational straight line GC, which is commensurable with the whole BG in square only (Step 6, Step 9), the remainder BC is an apotome (10.73), its whole being BG and its annex GC.

**Step 11.** Let BG be bisected at O (1.10), and with centre O and distance OB let the circle BKG be described (P3), of which BG is a diameter. Since GC is less than BG (Step 6), let there be fitted into the circle, from the point G, the straight line GK equal to GC (4.1), and let BK be joined (P1). The angle BKG, being an angle in a semicircle, is right (3.31); therefore the square on BG is equal to the squares on GK, KB (1.47), that is, to the squares on GC, KB. Let H denote the straight line KB. Thus the square on BG is greater than the square on GC by the square on H.

**Step 12.** Since, as ED is to DF, so is the square on BG to the square on GC (Step 6), and ED exceeds DF by FE (Step 2), while the square on BG exceeds the square on GC by the square on H (Step 11), therefore, convertendo, as DE is to EF, so is the square on BG to the square on H (5.19, Porism).

**Step 13.** But DE, EF are square numbers (Step 2); therefore DE has to EF the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence the square on BG also has to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BG is commensurable in length with H (10.9).

**Step 14.** Therefore BC is an apotome (Step 10) whose whole is BG and whose annex is GC; the square on the whole BG is greater than the square on the annex GC by the square on H (Step 11), a straight line commensurable in length with the whole BG (Step 13); and the whole BG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Step 1). Therefore BC is a first apotome (D10.3.1). Thus the first apotome BC has been found. Q.E.F.

**Path note.** The square numbers were fixed explicitly (9, 4, difference 5) rather than by appeal to the unnumbered lemma after 10.28, and the straight line H whose square is the excess of the square on BG over the square on GC was constructed by the semicircle method (4.1, 3.31, 1.47) rather than by citing the unnumbered lemma after 10.13, since lemmas carry no proposition numbers; this matches the convention used for 10.29, 10.30 and 10.49 in this run.

**USED:** D10.1.3, D7.18, 8.24, 10.6, D5.5, 1.3, 10.9, 10.12, D10.1.2, 10.73, 1.10, P3, 4.1, P1, 3.31, 1.47, 5.19, D10.3.1

result.statement: To find the second apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the rational straight line set out, and let GC be a straight line commensurable in length with A. Then GC is rational [D10.1.3]. Further, since GC is commensurable in length with A, the square on GC has to the square on A the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; therefore the square on GC is commensurable with the square on A [10.6], so that the square on GC is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 2.** Let two square numbers DE, EF be set out, DE being the greater, such that their difference FD (that is, DE less EF) is not a square number; for example, let DE be 9 (contained by 3 and 3) and EF be 4 (contained by 2 and 2), so that their difference FD is 5, which is not a square number [D7.18].

**Step 3.** Let it be contrived that, as the number FD is to the number DE, so is the square on CG to the square on GB [10.6, Por.], GB being drawn from G along the straight line GC in the direction of C. Then, inversely, as the square on GB is to the square on CG, so is the number DE to the number FD [5.7, Por.].

**Step 4.** Since the square on GB has to the square on CG the ratio which a number has to a number, the square on GB is commensurable with the square on CG [10.6]; hence GB and CG are commensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 5.** Since, as DE is to FD, so is the square on GB to the square on CG, then, by the definition of the same ratio, if equimultiples be taken of DE and of the square on GB, and equimultiples of FD and of the square on CG, the former alike exceed or alike fall short of the latter; taking each magnitude once, since DE exceeds FD, the square on GB exceeds the square on CG [D5.5]. Hence GB is greater than CG (for the square on the less of two straight lines is less than the square on the greater); therefore the point B falls beyond C, so that C lies between B and G and CG is a part of GB.

**Step 6.** Now the square on GB is commensurable with the square on CG, and the square on CG is commensurable with the square on A; therefore the square on GB is commensurable with the square on A [10.12]. Hence the square on GB is rational [D10.1.4], and GB, being commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2], is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 7.** But DE has not to FD the ratio which a square number has to a square number. For, if it had, then, since DE is square, FD would also be square [8.24]; but FD is not square. Therefore neither has the square on GB to the square on CG the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore GB is incommensurable in length with CG [10.9].

**Step 8.** Therefore GB, CG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. And from the rational straight line GB there has been subtracted the rational straight line CG commensurable with the whole in square only; therefore the remainder BC is an apotome [10.73], GB being the whole and CG the annex.

**Step 9.** I say next that BC is a second apotome. Let a square be constructed equal to the excess of the square on GB over the square on CG [2.14], and let H be its side; then the square on GB is greater than the square on CG by the square on H.

**Step 10.** Since, as the square on GB is to the square on CG, so is the number DE to the number FD, therefore, convertendo, as the square on GB is to the excess of the square on GB over the square on CG, that is, to the square on H, so is DE to the excess of DE over FD, that is, to EF [5.19, Por.].

**Step 11.** But DE and EF are both square numbers; therefore the square on GB has to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore GB is commensurable in length with H [10.9].

**Step 12.** Therefore the square on the whole GB is greater than the square on the annex CG by the square on a straight line H commensurable in length with the whole GB; and the annex CG is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out. Therefore the apotome BC is a second apotome [D10.3.2].

**Step 13.** Therefore the second apotome BC has been found. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To find the third apotome.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line A be set out [D10.1.3], and let three numbers E, BC, CD be set out which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but such that CB has to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; here D lies between B and C, so that BD is the excess of the number BC over the number CD. (Such numbers exist, e.g. E, BC, CD = 3, 8, 6, whence BD = 2 and CB : BD = 4 : 1.)

**Step 2.** By the porism to 10.6, let it be contrived that, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH [10.6].

**Step 3.** Since the square on A has to the square on FG the ratio which the number E has to the number BC, the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG [10.6]. The square on A is rational [D10.1.4]; therefore the square on FG is rational [D10.1.4], and FG, being commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2], is rational [D10.1.3]. But E has not to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence the square on A has not to the square on FG the ratio of a square number to a square number, so that A and FG are incommensurable in length [10.9].

**Step 4.** Again, since the square on FG has to the square on GH the ratio which the number BC has to the number CD, the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH [10.6]. The square on FG is commensurable with the square on A (Step 3); therefore the square on GH is commensurable with the square on A [10.12], hence rational [D10.1.4], and GH is rational [D10.1.3]. But BC has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence FG and GH are incommensurable in length [10.9]. Therefore FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 5.** Since CD is a part of BC, BC is greater than CD [CN5]; and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH; therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on GH [5.14], so that FG is greater than GH. From the rational straight line FG let the rational straight line GH, commensurable with FG in square only, be subtracted; the remainder FH is an apotome [10.73], FG being its whole and GH its annex.

**Step 6.** Since, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH [5.22]. But E has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; hence the square on A has not to the square on GH the ratio of a square number to a square number, so that A and GH are incommensurable in length [10.9]. Thus neither the whole FG (Step 3) nor the annex GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out.

**Step 7.** On FG let the semicircle FLG be described; since GH is less than the diameter FG (Step 5), let FL equal to GH be fitted into it [4.1], and let LG be joined. The angle FLG, being in a semicircle, is right [3.31]; therefore the square on FG is equal to the squares on FL, LG [1.47], that is, to the squares on GH, LG. Let K be equal to LG; then the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on K.

**Step 8.** Since, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, convertendo, as BC is to the excess BD, so is the square on FG to its excess over the square on GH, that is, as CB is to BD, so is the square on FG to the square on K [5.19].

**Step 9.** But CB has to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore the square on FG has to the square on K the ratio which a square number has to a square number, so that FG and K are commensurable in length [10.9]. Hence the square on the whole FG is greater than the square on the annex GH by the square on a straight line K commensurable in length with the whole FG.

**Step 10.** Therefore FH is an apotome (Step 5) of which neither the whole FG nor the annex GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Step 6), while the square on the whole is greater than the square on the annex by the square on a straight line commensurable with the whole (Step 9). Therefore FH is a third apotome [D10.3.3]. Thus the third apotome FH has been found. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To find the fourth apotome.
result.proof:
**Statement:** To find the fourth apotome.

**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line A be set out, and let BG be a straight line commensurable in length with A. Then BG is rational (D10.1.3). Moreover, since BG, A are commensurable in length, the square on BG has to the square on A the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), so the square on BG is commensurable with the square on A (10.6); hence the square on BG is rational (D10.1.4).

result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the rational straight line set out, and let CG be a straight line commensurable in length with A (for instance, equal to A). Then CG is rational [D10.1.3]. Moreover, since CG, A are commensurable in length, the square on CG has to the square on A the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9], so that the square on CG is commensurable with the square on A [10.6]; that is, the square on CG is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 2.** Set out two numbers DF, FE such that the whole DE has neither to DF nor to FE the ratio which a square number has to a square number (for instance DF = 1, FE = 2, so that DE = 3). Then FE has not to ED the ratio which a square number has to a square number either; for otherwise ED would have to FE the inverse ratio, which would again be a ratio of a square number to a square number.

**Step 3.** By the Porism to 10.6, from the straight line CG and the numbers FE, ED construct a straight line GB such that, as FE is to ED, so is the square on CG to the square on GB [10.6]; let GB lie in a straight line with GC, on the side of C.

**Step 4.** Since FE is less than ED, and as FE is to ED so is the square on CG to the square on GB, the square on CG is less than the square on GB [D5.5, taking each of the four magnitudes once]; hence CG is less than GB, so that C falls between B and G, and BC is what remains when GC is subtracted from BG.

**Step 5.** Since the square on CG has to the square on GB the ratio FE : ED, which is the ratio of a number to a number, the square on CG is commensurable with the square on GB [10.6]. But the square on CG is commensurable with the square on A (Step 1); therefore the square on GB is also commensurable with the square on A [10.12], that is, the square on GB is rational [D10.1.4]. Hence GB is commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2] and is therefore rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 6.** Since FE has not to ED the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 2), neither has the square on CG to the square on GB that ratio; therefore CG is incommensurable in length with GB [10.9]. On the other hand the squares on BG, GC are commensurable (Step 5), so that BG, GC are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Therefore BG, GC are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 7.** Therefore, GC being subtracted from the rational straight line BG, the remainder BC is an apotome [10.73], its whole being BG and its annex GC.

**Step 8.** It remains to show that BC is a fifth apotome. Describe a circle having BG as diameter, and into it fit the straight line BK equal to GC, which is possible since GC is less than BG [4.1]; join KG. The angle BKG, being in a semicircle, is right [3.31]; therefore the square on BG is equal to the squares on BK, KG, that is, to the squares on GC, KG [1.47]. Let H denote KG; then the square on BG is greater than the square on GC by the square on H.

**Step 9.** Since as FE is to ED so is the square on CG to the square on BG (Step 3), inversely, as ED is to FE so is the square on BG to the square on CG [5.7, Porism]. Therefore, convertendo, as ED is to the excess DF by which ED exceeds FE, so is the square on BG to the excess by which the square on BG exceeds the square on CG; that is, as ED is to DF, so is the square on BG to the square on H [5.19, Porism].

**Step 10.** But ED has not to DF the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 2); therefore neither has the square on BG to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BG is incommensurable in length with H [10.9].

**Step 11.** Thus BC is an apotome (Step 7) such that the square on its whole BG is greater than the square on its annex GC by the square on a straight line H incommensurable in length with the whole BG (Steps 8, 10), while the annex GC is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Step 1). Therefore BC is a fifth apotome [D10.3.5]; and it has been found. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 10.90
**Statement:** To find the sixth apotome.

**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line A be set out, and let three numbers E, BC, CD be set out such that no two of them have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; let D lie on BC, so that BD is the excess of BC over CD, and let CB also not have to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number. (Such numbers exist: for instance E = 2, BC = 6, CD = 3, whence BD = 3; the ratios 2 : 6 = 1 : 3, 6 : 3 = 2 : 1, 2 : 3 and CB : BD = 6 : 3 = 2 : 1 are none of them ratios of a square number to a square number.) Since CD is a part of BC, BC is greater than CD [CN5].

**Step 2.** By the Porism to 10.6, contrive a straight line FG such that, as the number E is to the number BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG; and again contrive a straight line GH, laid along GF from G, such that, as the number BC is to the number CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH [10.6].

**Step 3.** Since the square on A has to the square on FG the ratio which the number E has to the number BC, the square on A is commensurable with the square on FG [10.6]. Therefore FG is commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2], and A being rational, FG is rational [D10.1.3]. Further, since E has not to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, the square on A has not to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number (the two ratios being the same); therefore A is incommensurable in length with FG [10.9].

**Step 4.** Since the square on FG has to the square on GH the ratio which the number BC has to the number CD, the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH [10.6]; therefore FG and GH are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. And since BC has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on FG to the square on GH; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with GH [10.9].

**Step 5.** Since, as E is to BC, so is the square on A to the square on FG, and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, ex aequali, as E is to CD, so is the square on A to the square on GH [5.22]. Hence the square on A is commensurable with the square on GH [10.6], so GH is commensurable in square with A [D10.1.2] and is therefore rational [D10.1.3]. And since E has not to CD the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on A to the square on GH; therefore A is incommensurable in length with GH [10.9].

**Step 6.** Since BC is greater than CD (Step 1), and, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, it follows from the definition of the same ratio, taking each of the four magnitudes once, that the square on FG is greater than the square on GH [D5.5]. Hence FG is greater than GH (for the square on a lesser line is a part of the square on a greater, and so less than it), so that H falls between F and G, and FH is the remainder when GH is subtracted from FG.

**Step 7.** Now FG and GH are rational (Steps 3, 5), commensurable in square (Step 4) but incommensurable in length (Step 4), that is, commensurable in square only; and GH, the less, has been subtracted from FG, the greater. Therefore the remainder FH is an apotome [10.73], FG being the whole and GH the annex.

**Step 8.** Since the square on FG is greater than the square on GH (Step 6), let K be the side of a square equal to the excess of the square on FG over the square on GH [2.14], so that the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on K. Since, as BC is to CD, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, convertendo, as CB is to BD, so is the square on FG to the excess of the square on FG over the square on GH, that is, to the square on K [5.19]. But CB has not to BD the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on FG to the square on K, and so FG is incommensurable in length with K [10.9].

**Step 9.** Therefore the square on the whole FG is greater than the square on the annex GH by the square on a straight line K incommensurable in length with the whole FG (Step 8); and neither the whole FG nor the annex GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line A set out (Steps 3, 5). Therefore the apotome FH is a sixth apotome [D10.3.6]. Thus the sixth apotome FH has been found. Q.E.F.
